title: Tenant isolation for devices
summary: A Sparkplug payload names no organization, so a device's tenant is decided by the credential it connects with. The middle row gives each connection and gateway a broker identity confined to one group. The bottom row is how the runtime turns a packet on that group into rows of one organization. The top row is the same boundary for vendor devices, which get a broker of their own.

boxes.label: Connections and gateways
boxes.detail: A connection names a Sparkplug group, unique across all organizations, and a gateway names one edge node in it. Laravel generates the usernames (host-<uuid>, edge-<uuid>) and 48-character passwords; creating either needs Device.manage-connections.

boxes.label: BrokerProvisioner
boxes.detail: A gateway may publish births, data and deaths only as its own edge node in its connection's group, and subscribe only to commands addressed to it. The host identity, used by the runtime, may subscribe to that group's births, data and deaths and publish its commands. Nothing else is allowed.

boxes.label: broker-admin
boxes.detail: The only thing that changes broker security. It accepts PUT /clients with a token, checks the username prefix, the password length and that every rule is an allow on a spBv1.0 topic, then applies one identity at a time: disable, replace role and password, enable last. A failure in between leaves the identity disabled.

boxes.label: Platform broker
boxes.detail: TLS only, no anonymous access. Publish, receive and subscribe are denied by default, and each identity has its own role. Subscriptions match the authorized filter literally and delivery is checked per topic, so a subscription to # or spBv1.0/# is refused.

boxes.label: Gateway or device
boxes.detail: Connects over TLS with the credentials from its connection kit. Whatever group or edge node it puts in a topic, the broker only lets through the ones its identity was given.

boxes.label: Refused by the broker
boxes.detail: A publish as another edge node or into another group is not delivered, and a subscription outside the identity's rules is rejected. The release check proves tenant and gateway isolation against a real broker.

boxes.label: Runtime host connection
boxes.detail: Laravel hands the runtime every ready connection with its organization_uuid, group and host credentials. The runtime opens one TLS client per connection and subscribes to that group's six message types and nothing wider.

boxes.label: Group check
boxes.detail: The callback knows which connection delivered the message. It parses the topic and drops the packet unless its group is the connection's group. The payload is never asked who it belongs to.

boxes.label: Match the device
boxes.detail: A packet reaches a device only through a definition Laravel activated for exactly this connection, edge node and device ID. Laravel decides which device may hold a source: the source's own organization, or within one billing account a device moved or onboarded into another organization.

boxes.label: Stored rows
boxes.detail: Readings, latest values, diagnostics, the outbox row and usage are written with the definition's organization_uuid, and only while that definition is still the one applied for that organization. Every read names an organization_uuid too.

boxes.label: Tenant ingress broker
boxes.sub: Own port, own CA, default deny
boxes.detail: Vendor devices publish fixed topics, so two tenants would collide on a shared broker. adapter-manager runs one Mosquitto per tenant with its own published port and certificate authority, and gives each adapter source and each device credential rules for its own topics only.

boxes.label: Tenant adapter runtime
boxes.detail: One per tenant, with no host port and its admin API behind a token only the manager knows. Decoders run in a QuickJS sandbox. Output leaves through a platform-owned publisher that is an ordinary gateway on the platform broker: group adapters-<organization uuid>, edge node adapter-<adapter uuid>.

steps.text: Someone creates a connection (a Sparkplug group) or a gateway (an edge node in it). Laravel generates its broker username and password.
Laravel sends the identity and its allow rules to broker-admin. A gateway's rules name its own group and edge node, nothing else.
broker-admin applies them through Mosquitto's Dynamic Security control topic, which device clients cannot reach.
The device connects with those credentials. From now on the connection, not the payload, says whose device it is.
Anything outside the rules is refused by the broker: another group, another edge node, a wildcard subscription.
The runtime holds one client per connection, signed in as that connection's host, and receives only that group's messages.
Each message arrives with the connection it came through.
A topic whose group is not the connection's group is dropped. Otherwise the runtime looks for the device activated for this connection, edge node and device ID.
Readings are stored under the organization of that device's definition. Laravel chose it when the device was activated.
Vendor devices connect to their tenant's own ingress broker instead, and the tenant's adapter runtime decodes what they send.
The adapter publishes Sparkplug B as a gateway in group adapters-<organization uuid>, so from here it follows the same path.
